title: Reached Subgame Nash Restriction
body_html:
Reached Subgame Nash Restriction

Let $\Gamma$ be an extensive-form game, let $\sigma^\ast$ be a Nash equilibrium in mixed strategies or behavior strategies, and let $\Gamma(x)$ be a subgame. If the probability of reaching $x$ under $\sigma^\ast$ is positive, then the restriction of $\sigma^\ast$ to $\Gamma(x)$ is a Nash equilibrium of the subgame $\Gamma(x)$.

Lean Scope

The Lean target uses FiniteImperfectGame.reachableSubgameAt for $\Gamma(x)$, so the state space is restricted to the continuation below the subgame root. A faithful formalization also needs behavior strategies, mixed strategies, reach probabilities, expected payoffs, profile restriction to a subgame, and lifting or splicing lemmas showing that a profitable deviation in a positive-probability subgame induces a profitable deviation in the original game.

The Arena-based auxiliary theorem ExtensiveGame.IsBehaviorNashEq.restrictSubgame_of_payoffTransfer proves the Nash-restriction step from an affine payoff-transfer interface. The root-subgame special case ExtensiveGame.IsBehaviorNashEq.restrictSubgame_init is proved without this interface.

The newer finite imperfect-information layer now contains a concrete reachable-state subgame, chance-aware behavioral reach probabilities, fixed-root finite-horizon payoff decomposition lemmas, and the behavior-strategy theorem FiniteImperfectGame.IsBehaviorNashEqWithChance.restrictReachableSubgame_of_reachProb_pos_finiteHorizon. This theorem derives the payoff decomposition from the recursive semantics, using an explicit outside horizon and a root continuation horizon to represent the finite tree facts that the textbook leaves implicit.

The mixed-strategy direction is proved by FiniteImperfectGame.IsMixedNashEqWithChance.restrictReachableSubgame_of_reachProb_pos_textbook. It uses the footnote-style mixed splice together with FiniteImperfectGame.ReachedSubgameMixedPayoffTransfer, which packages the textbook equations (7.2)--(7.5), and then proves the cancellation step leading to the subgame Nash inequality.

References

  • [MSZ, Thm. 7.5] Maschler, Solan, and Zamir, Game Theory. A Nash equilibrium restricted to a subgame reached with positive probability remains a Nash equilibrium of that subgame.
